title: Toward Interpretable Quantum Generators for Financial Returns through Problem-Informed Circuit Design
authors: Huijie Guan, Xuanhao Wang, Shengbin Wang, Jiale Zhang, Jian Ding, Shuxin Xie, Dongdong Li, Jianjian Gao, Hantao Sun, Wenhao Chu
abstract: When used as function approximators, quantum circuits often lack interpretability and face a fundamental trade-off between expressivity and trainability. We propose a problem-informed framework for financial return generation that uses relational structure and symmetry-inspired parameter sharing to guide the construction of quantum circuits with few trainable parameters and empirically testable operator roles. We evaluate three quantum generator architectures, referred to as ZZ, directed ZZ-CRX, and structured time evolution, within a hybrid Wasserstein quantum generative adversarial network trained to generate 16-step Bitcoin return windows. Across circuits with one to four layers and one to eight trainable coefficients, these generators recover meaningful marginal and temporal distributional features, while single-layer configurations remain competitive with deeper variants. Across matched depths, independently trained ZZ-CRX configurations exhibit a predominantly downward shift in median leverage relative to ZZ, consistent with the intended directional role of the controlled-rotation construction. The small number of coefficients also enables direct landscape analysis, revealing competing parameter preferences between marginal and temporal objectives and helping to explain the difficulty of finding parameter settings that perform well on both. These results provide an initial demonstration that structural assumptions can guide the design of compact quantum generators and link circuit architecture to observable statistical behaviour, motivating more systematic and parameter-efficient approaches to quantum circuit construction.
summary: This work proposes a novel, problem-informed framework to build interpretable quantum generators for modeling financial returns using a QGAN. By embedding domain knowledge—such as expected correlations and asymmetries—into the quantum circuit structure, the authors demonstrate that compact circuits can capture complex statistical features. This advances the field by linking explicit structural assumptions directly to the observable performance of quantum models.
main_problem: The paper addresses the interpretability and trainability trade-off when using quantum circuits as function approximators for complex tasks like financial return generation.
main_result: The proposed problem-informed framework successfully guides the design of compact quantum generators that recover meaningful marginal and temporal distributional features of financial returns.
method: They employ a hybrid Wasserstein Quantum Generative Adversarial Network (QGAN) trained on financial data, guiding the quantum circuit design using structural assumptions like relational structure and symmetry-inspired parameter sharing.
model_or_system: The model uses quantum circuits (ZZ, directed ZZ-CRX, structured time evolution) to generate 16-step Bitcoin return windows. The circuit structure is explicitly informed by the statistical properties of the financial data.
key_observables: Marginal distribution fidelity, short-range absolute-return dependence, and median leverage shift.
important_parameters: Number of trainable coefficients (1 to 8) and circuit depth (1 to 4 layers).
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that structural assumptions derived from the physical problem (finance) can guide the design of compact, efficient quantum generators.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the workflow from empirical financial structure to mechanistic hypothesis, leading to operator construction and falsifiable predictions.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure moving from identifying the scientific problem (interpretability in QML) to proposing a problem-informed framework, detailing the QGAN setup and circuit design, presenting results on distributional recovery, and concluding with implications for systematic circuit design.
why_interesting: While applied to finance, the methodology of imposing physical/structural constraints (like symmetry or known correlations) to guide quantum circuit ansatz design is highly relevant for developing physically meaningful quantum machine learning models in AMO physics.
